decisions.quote: Experiment 1 succeeded in replicating the original finding by Jiang and Forster (2001)—namely, the existence of L2–L1 translation priming in an episodic recognition task— but failed to confirm the absence of priming in the L1–L2 condition in the same task.
decisions.reason: The authors explicitly state that Experiment 1 replicated Jiang and Forster's (2001) L2–L1 priming finding in episodic recognition (Experiment 1A) but failed to replicate the absence of L1–L2 priming in the same task (Experiment 1B), which is a mixed replication outcome rather than overall agreement with the general episodic L2 hypothesis.

decisions.quote: In this final experiment, a more powerful test of the episodic L2 hypothesis is carried out using a more robust form of priming, namely, repetition priming rather than translation priming. As explained earlier, it has been found that in an episodic recognition task, old words show strong masked repetition priming, but there is no priming for new words (Forster, 1985; Rajaram & Neely, 1992).
decisions.reason: Forster (1985) is cited as background literature establishing the known L1 repetition-priming baseline used to motivate a novel test of the episodic L2 hypothesis and its monolingual control group in Experiment 3, not as a target study being re-tested.

shipped.title_o: Cross-Language Priming Asymmetries in Lexical Decision and Episodic Recognition
shipped.outcome_quote: Overall, the results from these 3 experiments support the hypothesis that L2 words are represented in episodic memory.

blind_target.title: Cross-language priming asymmetries in lexical decision and episodic recognition.
blind_target.evidence_quote: Our first step is to establish the reliability of Jiang and Forster’s (2001) original results. To this end, we tested translation priming in a new sample of highly proficient Chinese–English bilinguals.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Experiment 1 succeeded in replicating the original finding by Jiang and Forster (2001)—namely, the existence of L2–L1 translation priming in an episodic recognition task— but failed to confirm the absence of priming in the L1–L2 condition in the same task.
